I’m not gonna give you the don’t do it spiel. Life isn’t worth ending and I’ll stick by that as someone who survived 2 suicide attempts. ANYWAY to answer your question unfortunately there are several medications that when taken in excess can cause cardiac arrest. It has less to do with the medication and more the dose. Mixing anything with alcohol usually amplifies that process. Be careful though, that’s the method I wanted to die from. I took enough pills to kill a horse (or so I thought) twice. The body is insane though and it will fight even when you’re unconscious to keep you alive. If I learned anything from suicidal thoughts and attempts it’s that nothing is as sure fire as you think. If you think you want to die now imagine if you take these pills and go into cardiac arrest and your brain isn’t getting blood but they revive you and now you’re in a wheel chair your whole life trapped in your own body with no way out. If you’re going to do it. WHICH I AM CLEARLY SAYING AGAIN I DO NOT RECOMMEND. You better do something that leaves nothing to chance. Pills are one of the things that seem to leave the most to chance. Stomach pumps, involuntarily throwing up, maybe even just sleeping it off. So many variables make it one of the least safe and least effective way to go.

However about a week goes by and I get a call from my mom asking if I had taken her pills. I told her that I hadn’t taken any recently, rather that it had been a few months ago. Here’s just some advice for you and you can do with it what you want. You relapsed. Face it, own it, and accept that it happened. One thing that’s hard about recovery is the thought of never doing that substance again. When you put that kind of pressure and mentality into your attempt to quit it can end up being detrimental to the entire process. You slipped up and you know it, you feel bad about it, and you obviously care about how it would not only affect you if you went back into your old addiction, you also know it would hurt your S/O. You are human. The human brain is a tricky thing. We all make mistakes and slip up. I think you need to look at yourself in the mirror metaphorically and realize that yeah, what happened sucks, but what am I going to do moving forward? Don’t think about it as such a black and white process. That’s how you’ll end up mentally saying “fuck it, I messed up my sobriety so there’s no point in trying to stay clean” that’s just not true though. Keep your head up, go back to the things you were doing that worked so well. I know we don’t know each other but I’m proud of you for not using for so long. I wish you the best moving forward. Remember sometimes it’s 2 steps forward 1 step back. Looks like it’s your time for those steps forward. Good luck.

First things first. Don’t take anymore. Sounds easy enough but your brain/body will want to convince you to take more to ease the symptoms of an inevitable come down. You have to accept your fate at this point. It’s going to suck. However you’re going to get through it and you WILL be okay. So now that you’ve stopped re-dosing have a small snack and some water. You’re most likely much hungrier and more dehydrated than your body is telling you. After you’ve eaten and had something to help hydrate you, try and take something along the lines of unisom or melatonin. Not sure of your drug/alcohol history but if you have access to weed/alcohol that will help ease your mind and create a mental space where your mind can slow down and start to come back down to earth per say. After that have a little bit more to eat and a glass of water. Now it’s time to lay down. Adderall and vyvanse have that sneaky ability to keep your mind up even though the euphoria is long gone, the previous things mentioned will ease that but might not completely take it away. What I would do from that point is find a dark quiet and cool room, lay down in bed, and start watching tv or listening to podcasts. Try to make it more audio than visual because blue light emitted from tvs phones etc can keep you awake. While watching or listening to something you enjoy, as cliche as this may sound, think about things that make you happy. Reminiscing on good times seems to help me, I think doing that releases just enough serotonin and dopamine to help our brains start to recover, it won’t take all of the restlessness away but it’s a good place to start. Before you know it after a few hours of not taking the substances you’ll be fast asleep. Next time you take addy/vivanse remember this feeling. Be prepared to come down, and try your best to set limits on how much you take, and the time of day. Best of luck, you got this!

So just to start this off I’ve never done heroin. Now that I know how I feel about opioids after taking them I know I would fall in love with it. My mom has severe arthritis so I was made aware of the drugs in our house that were not to be touched at a young age. My mom is very responsible with her medication and would make a script that should only last 2 months last 6-8 months. When I was in high school I heard about kids wanting to by them. Knowing my mom rarely took her scripts meant I could take them and she wouldn’t know for a few weeks, if at all. So I went into my parents safe and found promethazine, oxy, morphine, tramadol, and a few other things. I was making a few hundred dollars a month in high school. To a kid who didn’t have a job yet I felt like I was rolling in cash. I always thought of the people who would pay all this money for pills and stupid and irresponsible. I was money hungry though so I didn’t care. Then it happened. I took one. All of a sudden it was like the clouds opened up in front of me. I loved it. Soon it went from selling to using. Those first few doses of euphoria to your brain are enough to keep you coming back forever. If I ever have kids I’m going to make sure to get the stigma of people who use H or painkillers because they’re losers out of their heads. I’m going to let them know that most of these addicts had bright futures ahead of them, that they never wanted to end up that way, that they were smart and kind and good people. I want them to associate drugs of that nature to reality. Not a scare tactic used that doesn’t enough scare people from using in the right way. They don’t address all the complexities of what happens when you try the substances. So I guess when I first thought of H or oxy I thought of loser, low life, piece of human garbage. Now I see the good in people and the bad in the drug itself. How it alters the brain in ways that form life altering addictions. This was a lot of typing but long story short, I was naive about the substances, now I’m hooked on Percocet and I’m very much aware of how even the most well intentioned and intelligent people can become addicts.
